title: One teaspoon. A billion tons.
hook: One teaspoon of neutron-star matter could weigh around a billion tons.

claims.claim: One teaspoon of neutron-star matter could weigh around a billion tons on Earth.
claims.source: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center (NICER mission press release)
claims.exact_wording: "On Earth, one teaspoon of neutron star matter would weigh a billion tons."
claims.assumption: Interior density near nuclear density (~10^17 kg/m3); exact figure depends on where in the star the material is scooped (crust vs core; deep-interior estimates run to several billion tons).
claims.confidence: HIGH for order of magnitude (10^9 t); exact number density-dependent -> script uses 'around/could'
claims.wording_in_script: could weigh around a billion tons

claims.claim: A sugar cube of neutron star material would weigh about 1 trillion kilograms (1 billion tons).
claims.exact_wording: "One sugar cube of neutron star material would weigh about 1 trillion kilograms (or 1 billion tons) on Earth - about as much as a mountain."

claims.claim: A tablespoon of neutron star weighs more than 1 billion tons.
claims.exact_wording: "A tablespoon of neutron star weighs more than 1 billion tons (900 billion kg)."

claims.claim: A neutron star begins its life as a star between about 7 and 20 times the mass of our Sun.
claims.exact_wording: "A neutron star begins its life as a star between about seven and 20 times the mass of our sun."
claims.assumption: Progenitor mass window for core-collapse supernovae.
claims.wording_in_script: up to twenty times the mass of our Sun

claims.claim: When the fuel runs out, gravity crushes the core in under a second.
claims.source: NMSU Astronomy lecture; expert answer with free-fall timescale 0.1-1.0 s
claims.exact_wording: "In less than a tenth of a second, the core of the star compresses to a radius of 20 kilometers and its density rises to that of the atomic nucleus." (free-fall time ~0.1-1.0 s per physics.stackexchange.com/questions/110460)
claims.wording_in_script: gravity crushed the core in under a second

claims.claim: The star explodes as a core-collapse supernova; the core keeps collapsing into a neutron star.
claims.exact_wording: "Eventually, the implosion bounces back off the core, expelling the stellar material into space, forming the supernova. What's left is an ultra-dense object called a neutron star."
claims.wording_in_script: The star exploded as a supernova - but the core kept collapsing

claims.claim: Up to twice the Sun's mass squeezed into a sphere 12 miles (20 km) across, the size of a city.
claims.exact_wording: "What remains is an ultra-dense sphere only about 12 miles (20 kilometers) across, the size of a city, but with up to twice the mass of our sun squeezed inside."
claims.wording_in_script: two Suns' worth of mass packed into a sphere the size of a city

claims.claim: Electrons and protons are crushed together, creating a sea of neutrons; neutron degeneracy pressure stops the collapse.
claims.exact_wording: Space.com: "the negatively-charged electrons and positively-charged protons that comprise the iron nuclei in this stellar core are crushed together, creating a sea of uncharged, or neutral neutrons". NASA Imagine: "newly-created neutrons can stop the collapse, leaving behind a neutron star."
claims.wording_in_script: protons and electrons are crushed into a sea of neutrons

claims.claim: Deep-interior teaspoon estimates run higher (up to ~4-6 billion tons).
claims.source: Secondary websites (e.g. sealycvb.org) - DISCOVERY ONLY, not evidence
claims.exact_wording: Varies by source; '4 billion tonnes' quoted for deep interior.
claims.assumption: Density at the star's core rather than crust.
claims.confidence: LOW - noted only inside c1's assumption column

source_hierarchy_rule: Tier 1: NASA/ESA/scientific institutions/peer-reviewed. Tier 2: reputable science publications. Tier 3: discovery/corroboration only, never primary evidence.

script.text: One teaspoon of neutron-star matter could weigh around a billion tons.
It comes from a neutron star - the dead core of a giant star.
A star that burned up to twenty times the mass of our Sun.
When the fuel ran out, gravity crushed the core in under a second.
The star exploded as a supernova - but the core kept collapsing.
Until two Suns' worth of mass packed into a sphere the size of a city.
So dense, protons and electrons are crushed into a sea of neutrons.
Scoop a teaspoon of that? Around a billion tons.
